planting.note: Plant chitted seed tubers once soil is workable and frost risk is receding; this first-early variety bulks quickly for an early summer harvest.

directions: Plant certified seed tubers about 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill as shoots emerge. Arran Pilot was bred on the Isle of Arran by farmer-breeder Donald MacKelvie, released in 1930, and quickly became one of Britain's most widely grown first-early potatoes thanks to its round, white-skinned tubers with shallow eyes and pure white flesh that boils to a smooth, waxy texture. Reliable heavy cropping and an undemanding nature kept it in commercial and garden use for decades, and it remains one of the most recognizable heirloom first earlies in the UK seed trade today.

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers in hilled rows once soil has warmed following the last frost; this second-early variety needs a bit longer than Arran Pilot to bulk fully.

directions: Plant certified seed tubers in hilled rows once soil has warmed after the last frost. Arran Banner was bred by Donald MacKelvie on the Isle of Arran and introduced commercially around 1927 as a second-early variety, producing round-to-oval tubers with smooth, pale yellow to light tan skin, shallow eyes, and creamy white flesh that cooks to a firm, waxy texture well suited to boiling and salads. It is a heavy yielder but, like many older potato cultivars, carries little resistance to late blight, so gardeners in wet climates should monitor foliage closely and harvest promptly once the tops die back.

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once the ground is workable in spring; Arran Comet bulks very early, so space generously for its vigorous early top growth.

directions: Plant certified seed tubers in well-drained soil once the ground is workable in spring, spacing generously for the vigorous early top growth. The last of Donald MacKelvie's long series of Arran-prefixed introductions, Arran Comet was released in the mid-1950s and is valued for very early bulking and high yields of long, oval, white-skinned tubers with white to cream flesh. It has long been grown as a popular garden first early across Wales, Scotland, and England, prized for its flavor whether boiled or fried, though its short dormancy means stored tubers sprout sooner than longer-keeping maincrop types.

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers after the last frost once soil has warmed; this long-season maincrop needs the full growing season to bulk and cure for storage.

directions: Plant certified seed tubers after the last frost once soil has warmed, allowing a long full season for this maincrop variety to bulk and mature. Arran Consul was bred by Donald MacKelvie from a cross of President and Flourball, released in 1925, and became known as one of the best-keeping potatoes of its era, with oblong tubers, light yellow skin, and dry, floury, off-white flesh. Its excellent storage life and dense texture made it historically important for commercial chip production and even for export to Spain in the mid-twentieth century, and it remains a traditional long-season floury maincrop choice for gardeners wanting real cellar-keeping staying power.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost; train the vigorous bee-pollinated vines on a trellis or allow them to ramble.

directions: Direct sow seeds after the soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing plants about a foot apart along a trellis or allowing room to ramble. Nezhin cucumber (also spelled Nezhinsky) is a bee-pollinated heirloom developed through generations of folk selection on the mineral-rich marshland soils around Nizhyn in northern Ukraine, where it became the foundation of a renowned regional pickling industry. The oblong, black-spined fruit are densely covered in coarse tubercles and are harvested small for the crisp, aromatic pickles the variety is famous for across Ukraine and the wider former Soviet Union. It tolerates cool swings and dry spells better than many modern slicing cucumbers, reflecting its long history of open-field cultivation without irrigation.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
Oregon State University Extension — Cucumber Growing Guide

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost; this very short-season landrace tolerates cooler conditions better than most cucumbers.

directions: Direct sow seeds once the soil has warmed after the last frost, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Murom cucumber (Muromskiy) is among the oldest named Russian cucumber landraces, tracing to the Vladimir region around the city of Murom and documented in wide cultivation there since at least the 19th century. It is remarkably early and cold-tolerant for a cucumber, often setting its small, knobby, pale- and dark-green-streaked fruit within about a month of sowing — a trait that made it valuable in Russia's short growing seasons before it faded from wide cultivation and was later recognized by Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a variety at risk of disappearing. The compact fruit are harvested young for fresh eating and traditional Russian pickling, with a reputation for exceptional crispness that once made it an export item to Germany under the generic name 'Russian cucumber.'
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
Oregon State University Extension — Cucumber Growing Guide

planting.note: Direct sow in deeply worked soil 3-6 weeks before the last frost; thin well since this variety needs ample room to form its large storage roots.

directions: Direct sow seeds about 1/2 inch deep in deeply worked, fertile soil 3-6 weeks before the last frost, thinning to give roots enough room to swell. Bordo 237 (also transliterated Bordeaux 237) is a mid-season beet selected in the former Soviet Union from Western European 'Bordeaux' blood-red beet stock and remains one of the most widely grown beet cultivars across Russia and Ukraine today, prized above all as the classic beet for borscht. The globe-shaped to slightly flattened roots develop deep burgundy-red flesh with no internal white rings or zoning, holding color and sweetness well through long cooking. Roots can be pulled young for greens and baby beets at around ten weeks, but for the dense, storage-quality roots the variety is best known for, allow the fuller season to pass before the main harvest.
sources: Russian State Register of Breeding Achievements (Gosreestr)
